title: Krishna Questions the Indra Sacrifice
story:
When the cowherds of Vrindavan turned the whole village over to the work of a great sacrifice, only one person in it came forward to ask what the work was for — and he was the person who least needed an answer.

Krishna had come in from the forest and found the elders gathered, his father Nanda at their head, deep in the bustle of a ceremony, the air loud with preparation. He did not stand apart and instruct them. Instead he came before the elders and bowed low, the way a boy comes to his father when he wants to be taught, and he asked.

"Tell me, father," he said, "what is this ceremony you have undertaken? What is its fruit, and for whom is it meant, and by what means is it to be accomplished?"

Four questions, and none of them small. He did not ask what the rite was called, or how it was done, or when it had begun. He asked what it was for, what it would produce, who would receive it, and how the whole thing was to be brought about. It was the question of someone who wanted not the shape of the ceremony but its heart.

His eagerness was plain to everyone there, and it was real; he asked as one who truly wished to hear the answer, not as one who already possessed it. Whatever the elders made of the question, they could not doubt the asking.

And the question carried a second edge, which he let show. People perform their rites whether they understand them or not, he said. A man who goes through the motions without knowing, and a man who acts with understanding, are not in the end doing the same thing. So before anything else he wanted to know what the elders had settled upon, and why. It was a challenge, gently made, but a challenge all the same — and every elder there felt its edge.

It was the kind of question Vrindavan had not stopped to ask in a very long time. The sacrifice had come down from the elders' fathers, and from their fathers before them, season after season. The seasons turned, the rains came, the fires were lit, the offering went up — and that, for as long as anyone remembered, had been reason enough. Until a boy stood among them and asked, gently, what all of it was for.

The elders had no cause to refuse him. And so the question hung in the air over the village — simple, unsettling, and not nearly as easy to answer as it had first appeared.
reflection: The striking thing is the posture: the one who knows everything comes to be taught, and his question does its work not by declaring an answer but by asking the elders to look at what they have always done without ever having to say why.
next_story_tease: But far above Vraja, the god to whom that sacrifice had always belonged was about to hear that it had been taken from him.
hero_scene: Young Krishna standing with bowed head before Nanda and the gathered elders of Vraja, asking about the great sacrifice being prepared while the village bustles with offerings around them.
